vignette:
She is a 66-year-old South Asian widow who has spent most of her life working with her hands and keeping herself busy. For years, she works in retail, a job that gives her structure and a reason to get out of bed early. She is polite with customers, careful with change, and known by coworkers as dependable. In many ways, she has learned to live quietly and to carry hardship without drawing attention to herself.

The assault happens later in life, after she has already weathered other losses, including the death of her husband. She does not describe that period as dramatic; it is the ordinary kind of evening that makes the memory feel even more unbearable. She is alone when a man rapes her, and afterward the world feels altered in a way she cannot fully put into words. In the days that follow, she moves through her home as if she is borrowing someone else's life. She washes herself repeatedly, but never feels clean. She cannot sleep for more than an hour or two at a time, and when she does drift off, she wakes with a start, her body braced before her mind has caught up. She keeps lights on at night and checks locks more than once, then again, because certainty never quite comes.

At first she tries to stay as normal as possible. She returns to work because she believes she has to. Retail gives her a script to follow: greet the customer, straighten the shelves, ring up purchases, smile when appropriate. She finds that the routine helps during the day, but only barely. In the store, she startles easily when someone comes up behind her or speaks too suddenly. Certain men are harder to look at, especially if they resemble her attacker in build, age, or the way they stand too close. She feels her chest tighten and her hands go cold, and she has to focus on the register keys so that no one notices she is fighting to remain present. At times she hears a voice or catches a smell that pulls her back so sharply that for a few seconds she cannot tell where she is. She has to remind herself to breathe, to look at the price tags, to name the aisle she is standing in.

The memories do not come as a neat story. They arrive in fragments: the pressure of his weight, the sound of her own breathing, the helpless shock that made her feel outside her body. She avoids anything that might stir those sensations. She stops taking the route home that passes the park where she once used to sit with her husband. She no longer answers the door unless she is certain of who is there. She avoids being alone after dark and will sometimes ask a relative to stay on the phone with her while she is getting ready for bed. She feels ashamed that she cannot simply "move on," and this shame makes her withdraw further. Her family means well, but she rarely tells them what is happening inside her. She has long been the one who endures, and she does not know how to become the kind of person who asks for comfort.

Her grief for her husband and the rape become tangled together. She misses the version of herself who once felt safe in the world, even if that safety was never perfect. Since the assault, she has little appetite and often forgets to eat until late in the day. She feels irritable in a way that surprises her; a careless remark from a customer or a coworker can leave her shaky and silent for hours. Some days she feels numb rather than distressed, as if her feelings have been placed behind glass. Other days the sadness comes hard and fast, and she sits on the edge of her bed after work with the same clothes still on, unable to gather the energy to change.

Now, months later, she continues to go to work, care for her household, and keep her appointments, but everything requires more effort. She measures each day by how long she can stay steady before the fear rises again. She is not the same woman she was before the assault, and she knows it in the way she locks the door, in the way she scans a room, in the way she pauses before entering her own home as if asking it whether it is safe to come inside.
